answerSheet.form: Any device you expect to use soon that is not in ALN's kit, such as iPads or laptops for GMs. Name it, or “none”.

readings.text: A standalone game may have no GM tablet at all: your words “gm and/or player scanners” read that way, so player scanners alone would be a game the engine allows; this one reading covers GM scanners alone, player scanners alone, and both together.
Your words “a device goes down mid-game” include the show machine itself, so the game must go on without it too. How it goes on is the question “The show machine fails mid-game” above.

One pack can be played networked on one night and standalone on another. The pack says only which of its effects the game cannot run without. Your words do not say who decides which way tonight's game runs: the designer, in the pack, or whoever sets up the night. Today the GM picks on the tablet at the start, and ALN's one pack plays either way. The agent reads your decision as keeping that.

A networked game that loses its show machine and carries on from its devices stays the networked game it was declared as. It does not become a standalone game, and your decision “[[dec:standalone-games-declared-never-mixed]]” does not change: no device is on a show machine, so nothing is mixed. When a machine is back, the devices' records are joined into the game's record.

When the show machine dies and the kit has no second machine, the game still carries on with less (no video, music, lights or TV) wherever the game can be played that way, so the engine may not make a second machine a requirement for it. A game that needs the show machine by its nature, as your second game does, may end in an orderly way instead, and every GM tablet says so. Your words “For more or less all use cases” and “if at all possible” read that way.

calls.title: Four readings of earlier decisions are confirmed
calls.call: Four earlier decisions are read as overtaken by later ones, as the decision record reads them: each build area no longer starts with its proof test failing on today's engine, unless the move from today's engine changes it in place ([[dec:one-program-design-half-then-build-half]], [[dec:build-the-test-rig-when-building-starts]]); the design rounds go by decision, not one design choice per question, the four questions on the game's live facts all bear on the first decision and are designed together there, and the nine questions serve as checks on each design ([[dec:the-nine-questions-the-pass-answers]], [[dec:five-documents-the-design-half-hands-over]], [[dec:when-the-design-half-is-finished]], [[dec:design-top-down-hardest-to-reverse-choices-first]]); the published protocol takes the place of the drafted message lists among the handover documents ([[dec:one-published-protocol-and-an-outside-test-bench]]); and the rig reproducing each finding marked for live proof is no longer a condition for ending the design half.
calls.why: Each reading follows from a later decision of yours that set the order of the work. Nothing a player, GM or designer meets changes; only how the pass runs. The earlier wordings stay in the record's history.

calls.title: The quality targets' numbers are sorted, not asked
calls.call: Each number a quality target needs is sorted as one of three kinds. An engine requirement or limit, which the engine states the same for every production and the tests measure (a tablet back under its name within five seconds; the minutes from publish to playing; how fast a scan is answered; how many scans each kind of device keeps while offline; how many copies one machine carries). A production's setting, which each production makes for itself with ALN's as the first set (power-on to a running show; set-up time; how long records are kept; the kit's devices and phones; a scanner's first sync). A technical default the agent proposes and a production may change (how the program watcher retries; how long before a screen says the engine is silent; the machine's load, memory, disk and temperature limits; how long data is kept until a production sets its own). Where an engine requirement has no value yet, the agent proposes an order of size now, chosen for what a GM or a player notices and marked proposed, and the measured value in the design round that builds it, which comes to you in that round's review. Each design also states its own time from power back to a running game, because that time decides whether a restart is fallback enough. The sorting is on each target on [[page:requirements]] and in the review below, where each default stands with its reason.
calls.why: You said many of these numbers are “stuff that the engine itself should be relatively agnostic about” ([[dec:the-engine-says-what-is-fixed-and-what-each-production-sets]]). A limit the engine is sized for is measured, not decided, and a production's numbers are that production's. The split is the agent's reading of your words, made as its call; it stands unless you overrule it. How the requirements are grouped is the agent's to propose and yours to overrule.

calls.title: The missing standalone declaration is a design flaw of its own
calls.call: [[flaw:N1]] stays a design flaw of its own, holding the eight findings from the review of standalone games, rather than joining [[flaw:C9]], [[flaw:C11]] and [[flaw:C14]].
calls.why: Three other design choices (what each fact does between games, one answer per question, how old a copy is) need the declared fact as an input and would otherwise each invent their own answer. How findings are grouped is the agent's analysis.

calls.title: A standalone game follows the rule you ratified for missing equipment
calls.call: The pack already says what the show needs and how much each need matters: “block the show” or “skip it”. A standalone game has none of the services the show machine runs. So the same rule applies. A need marked “skip it” reads grey, as not installed tonight. A need marked “block the show” keeps the game from starting standalone and names the need, unless the GM types the override that rule allows. In the design tool the designer sees the same result as a badge when the pack is checked against a set-up with no show machine. A rule that cannot run on a device alone is treated the same way. ALN's pack marks every one of its needs “skip it” today, so ALN stays playable standalone.
calls.why: You ratified this rule on 2026-09-04 for equipment a venue leaves at home, and the targets “[[qt:QT6]]” and “[[qt:QT37]]” already say the grey half. A standalone game is the same case. A reading that follows from your earlier decision is the agent's call. Where the check runs when there is no show machine is for the design rounds.

calls.title: In a standalone game, whoever holds the GM tablet holds the game's controls
calls.call: In a standalone game nothing checks a login, so whoever holds the GM tablet holds the game's controls.
calls.why: The target “[[qt:QT31]]” gives the controls to staff who log in, and a standalone tablet decides alone. The agent states the consequence so you can overrule it.

calls.title: Who wins when two tablets claimed one token while apart
calls.call: First come, first served, as today. The first claim the engine accepts holds the token. A later claim for the same token shows as a red row with its reason, and the GM can overrule it by deleting one sale and entering the other. For scans kept while a tablet was cut off, the engine keeps both the order in which they reached it and the time each tablet stamped. Which of the two counts as first is for the design round.
calls.why: Your pack already declares that a token is claimed once, and the engine already gives it to the first team, so this follows from an earlier rule. A game can declare another rule in its pack later.

calls.title: Every refused GM scan attempt is recorded
calls.call: The engine records every attempt and its answer, kept as long as the production keeps its records ([[qt:QT30]]), and shows it nowhere until a feature needs it.
calls.why: It changes nothing anyone sees. A fact not kept is lost for good, the after-game tools can read it later, and it helps sort out a game afterwards when a device failed mid-game ([[dec:no-technical-failure-stops-a-game]]). You asked for the agent's view on this, and the view is the call.

calls.title: The design allows other hardware; what the first release requires comes with the build plan
calls.call: Every class of device in ALN's kit can be replaced in the design: the show machine, the GM's station, the players' devices, the public screens, the room's programs and the network. The panel gets ALN's kit as the first production's hardware, as facts. The GM app keeps taking typed codes on a device with no NFC, as it does today. The build plan proposes, for each stage of the roadmap, the hardware the engine names as required and the hardware it supports, and brings that list to you.
calls.why: Your words settle the design side: “we should build the fundamental architecture to allow flexibility with the hardware down the line”. Your decision leaves the line itself to the design rounds and the build plan ([[dec:the-engine-is-hardware-flexible-the-roadmap-sets-the-bounds]]). What an adopter must buy at each stage is yours, and it comes to you then, when the cost of each choice is known.

calls.title: The tap promise is to be split in two
calls.call: [[promise:J3]] is to be split into “Every tap gets its answer” and “The night can be told afterwards”. The split is made after the panel's synthesis, so you and the panel read the same ten. Until then [[page:requirements]] shows it as one promise, and the count of ten stands.
calls.why: The two halves serve different people at two moments, the GM or player at the tap and the director after the show, and share no part. How the requirements are worded and grouped is the agent's call ([[dec:the-decisions-page-holds-only-your-decisions]]).

calls.title: Three choices about how the promises are worded
calls.call: The venue promise stays one, titled “[[promise:J8]]”, with standalone games in its first sentences and another production fitting the engine to its own venue and hardware named in them. Proof and release stay one promise, as the title of “[[promise:J10]]” has it. Neither “[[promise:J4]]” nor “[[promise:J2]]” says how the state of the video, music and lights reaches a screen. That is for the design rounds.
calls.why: The venue promise: a separate promise for running in any set-up would own no part, and your decision on what each production sets adds a person to its sentences, not a second promise. Proof and release: whether two moments sit in one promise or two is wording, and the product question inside release day is yours, under “Release day: what must update together, and how long older devices work”. The room's state: where a sentence goes is wording, and the choice behind it belongs to the design rounds. How the requirements are worded and grouped is the agent's call ([[dec:the-decisions-page-holds-only-your-decisions]]).

calls.title: The panel's three lenses
calls.call: Three architects. The state lens becomes “state, authority and keeping the game going through a failure”, with [[dec:no-technical-failure-stops-a-game]] as its first test, and it also asks how the engine drives outside programs that crash, hang or answer late. The growth lens names hardware flexibility and both kinds of extension, and asks whether an add-on runs inside the engine or as a separate program whose failure cannot stop the engine. “Living with it” stays. No fourth architect. Each architect is also asked for more, and the brief on Design lists all of it. Six of the asks are these. What the design leaves out, and which requirement that costs. For each mechanism, what must be kept working or kept equal for years because of it. For the state and the extension decisions, one rejected alternative that differs in kind. Any requirement that says how to build something and not only what is needed, with the need behind it. The largest kit the design carries on ALN's show machine before it needs rework, and what gives way first. And what keeping phones and hardware scanners equal in ability costs the design.
calls.why: How the panel runs is the agent's call ([[dec:the-decisions-page-holds-only-your-decisions]]). You called a paused game “the worst possible scenario”, so the state lens now names keeping the game going. The three architects run on the same model and read the same folder and the same agenda, so they are independent in what they have read and not in habit. The added asks make the three proposals differ in kind and show what each leaves out. Naming a subject in a lens costs nothing; a fourth architect costs two more agents and a longer synthesis, and three is your decision.

calls.title: Each architect lists the decisions before seeing the agenda
calls.call: Each architect first writes their own list of the hardest decisions to reverse, from the goal, the requirements, the setting and your decisions. Only then do they open the six, say where their list differs and why, and write their design. This applies if you give the blind round the agenda, under “What the panel gets in its blind round”.
calls.why: The six are how the agent running the pass divided the problem, and you approved them on 2026-11-01. A panel that starts from them answers inside that division. One more step for each architect shows whether three outsiders would divide it the same way. How the panel runs is the agent's call.

calls.title: The second round reads today's code
calls.call: A fact sheet first, then the code and its component guides, to read only.
calls.why: Your decision gives the second round today's engine as facts and does not say in what form; the form is method. The code is the most exact fact about today's engine. It can pull a design toward small changes to today's engine, so the architects revise their own blind proposals rather than start again from the code.

review.title: The ten promises
review.what: What each person can count on at a given moment. Flag any that is missing, doubled or wrongly put; their wording is the agent's call, listed above. Two additions from version 9 stay in them for your review: the pack promise's two clauses (a second designer's game runs on the same engine; every device plays the same version of the pack and shows which) and the second half of the roles promise (only staff who log in start, pause, end or reset a game, run show control or change a score).

review.title: The quality targets
review.what: Forty-seven targets under twelve qualities, each a situation that can be tested. Flag what is wrong or missing. Twenty-two of the forty-seven rest on rulings you have already made. Twenty-five are proposed or partly settled, and seventeen carry a number, sorted below. Read those first; the rest are there if you want them. Four targets are new in this version and proposed: “[[qt:QT45]]”, “[[qt:QT46]]”, “[[qt:QT47]]” and “[[qt:QT48]]”. Several others are reworded after the review you asked for. Each number a target needs is sorted below as an engine requirement or limit, a production's setting (ALN's first) or a technical default. None waits on you as a decision now. Where an engine requirement has no value yet, its line gives the order of size the agent proposes, and the measured value comes to you in the design round that builds it.
numbers: The size the panel designs for: shows of a few dozen devices, as ALN's, players' phones included. That is the setting you approved on 2026-11-01. The largest kit the engine supports is measured on each machine, not chosen. Say so if you expect shows where the players' own phones take the count well past that, and the panel designs for the larger number.
[[qt:QT1]]: how long the engine may take from power back to a running show. A production's setting; the engine states its own restart time on each supported machine.

[[qt:QT2]]: how many restarts the program watcher tries, and over how long. A technical default. Today the shared program watcher, which starts the music player, the video player and three monitors (sound routing, Bluetooth and playback), restarts a program that died without printing anything four times, waiting ten seconds and doubling the wait each time (10, 20, 40, then 80 seconds), and shows red at the fifth failure. A program that printed anything before it died is restarted after five seconds, without limit. The video player uses the same watcher, set to a fixed three seconds, and the TV's browser has no watcher. The agent starts from the shared watcher: it serves every production the same way and starts from today's code. Ten seconds for the controls to come back: an engine requirement, from the promise's test.
[[qt:QT3]]: five seconds for a tablet to be back under its own station name. An engine requirement.

[[qt:QT5]]: how long after the engine goes silent a screen must say so. A technical default, sorted by kind of connection, and the engine states the longest delay it allows. The agent proposes a few seconds for a GM tablet or a scoreboard screen, which hold a live connection, and ten seconds for a player scanner, which checks at intervals. Ten seconds is how often both player scanners check today, and it is slow for a GM tablet. The value trades network traffic against how fast a screen admits its numbers are old, and a production may change it. Today a scoreboard screen's clock keeps counting by itself when the engine goes silent. This target proposes that it stops and shows as unconfirmed. Say if you would rather it keep counting.

[[qt:QT9]]: the minutes from publish to playing. An engine requirement; a change moves only the small pack, and its media moves ahead of time, so the time does not grow with a production's media. No value yet: the agent proposes a few minutes as the order of size.
[[qt:QT13]]: how long the venue technician may need from an unpacked kit to a go. A production's setting.
[[qt:QT14]]: how long from power on to a running show. A production's setting; the engine states its own start time on each supported machine.
[[qt:QT19]]: how long a newcomer may need to make and prove a first small change. An engine requirement. No value yet: the agent proposes a few hours, inside one working day, as the order of size.

[[qt:QT30]]: how long each kind of data is kept, per game. A production's setting, and the engine keeps nothing past it. The default the engine ships with, which every later operator inherits until a production sets its own, is a technical default: the agent proposes 90 days for every kind of data.

[[qt:QT33]]: the kit size. A production's setting, ALN's being tonight's kit; the engine states the largest kit it supports, measured on each supported machine. The scan answer time, the message delivery time and half a second for a video to report started: engine requirements. The first two have no value yet: as orders of size the agent proposes well under a second for a scan's answer and about a second for a live message to reach every tablet. The machine's load, memory, disk and temperature limits: technical defaults proposed for each supported machine, with ALN's show machine as the first, because the engine is meant to be flexible about hardware and no one machine's limits are the engine's.
[[qt:QT34]]: the number of player phones one kit carries. A production's setting, measured on its own machine and wifi.

[[qt:QT35]]: the longest acceptable first sync for a hardware scanner. A production's setting (ALN's first value is today's, 5 to 15 minutes for 30 to 40 MB); the engine states how fast each kind of scanner downloads.

[[qt:QT40]]: how many scans each kind of device must keep while offline. An engine limit the engine states for each kind of device (today both player scanners keep 100 and drop the oldest without a word). A device that reaches its limit says so on its screen and never drops a scan silently. If a game may carry on without the show machine, each design says how many scans a device keeps and what that covers.

[[qt:QT42]]: how long going back to the release before may take. An engine requirement, stated for each supported machine. No value yet: the agent proposes the same night, before the next game, as the order of size, which is what the target's title asks.

[[qt:QT43]]: how many copies of the engine one machine must carry at once. An engine requirement; whether it is one or two during a show waits on your question “Where the trial copy runs while a show runs”.
[[qt:QT44]]: how long after a failure every GM tablet must show the fallbacks. An engine requirement. No value yet: the agent proposes about ten seconds as the order of size.

[[qt:QT46]]: how long before the engine stops a mechanic that fires without end, or marks a hung program down. An engine requirement. No value yet: the agent proposes about ten seconds as the order of size.

review.title: The extension cases
review.what: Twenty-eight ways the platform must grow, each marked as one of your two kinds of extension or neither; your two examples are among them ([[ex:EX25]], [[ex:EX26]]), with another production adopting the engine ([[ex:EX27]]) and other hardware ([[ex:EX28]]). Flag any way of growing you plan that is missing, before the panel's folder is built.

review.title: The standing rules
review.what: The roadmap's standing constraints, one plain line each. They did not change on 2026-11-02, because the roadmap did not; flag any you no longer hold. The review you asked for found each one sound. It also found that the rule that phones and hardware scanners stay equal in ability costs the most: every action a pack may declare must also run on a small board updated by cable. Each architect is asked what it costs their design, and the rule stays unless you say otherwise.

designRounds.text: How the engine holds the game's state: the facts of a running game that can change during it, where each is kept, how every screen's copy of them stays true, and how the game's state carries on through a failure and comes back together afterwards.

The published protocol's form: the protocol itself is decided; this round settles how each message and each file that crosses the engine's edge (what a device may ask, what the engine answers, what it tells screens, and the files that carry a game or a night) is defined and versioned, the version rules against your release-day answers, and how each kind of device gets its pass.

Where authority lives across devices, offline and standalone included: which place decides each fact when a tablet is cut off, when the show machine fails, and when a game runs with no show machine at all; and how what you choose under “A GM tablet cut off from the engine” is built.

How games and venues extend the engine: what a pack and a venue profile can declare, which of your two kinds of extension each change is, where a developer adds support for a device, a program, a scoring model or a content source, and where a production's own settings live.

How one engine runs as many separate copies: the show's copy, a trial copy and a test run on one machine, each keeping its own files, network ports and settings, a second kit on another machine, and a copy on different hardware; and how a release is put on a kit and taken back. Where the designer's trial copy runs is your question “Where the trial copy runs while a show runs” above.

How today's engine moves to the new design: the build plan starts with a thin first version of the new design on the new test bench; whether today's engine is instead changed in place is part of this decision.

later.text: Where the night's set-up holds “this game is standalone”: the venue profile (the earlier candidate favours it), the game's record or each device. Whether the pack may say it too waits on a reading you are asked to confirm, on who says which way tonight's game runs ([[page:decisions#readings|the readings to confirm]]). It is decided in the round on where authority lives across devices.

Getting facts onto screens: one delivery part for every fact, or the parts behind each promise delivering their own facts in one shared format. It is decided in the round on how the engine holds the game's state.

The life of a game: one lifecycle part that alone moves the game and resets every part, or a table each part reads and applies itself. It is decided in the round on how the engine holds the game's state.

The game rules as one shared body of code that the engine and the tablet both run, or two bodies kept equal by tests. It is decided in the rounds on how the engine holds the game's state and on where authority lives across devices.

The equipment's interface: one per kind of thing the room can do (play a video, light a scene), or one per outside program. It is decided in the round on how the engine holds the game's state, or in a round of its own on how the engine drives the room if you add that decision.

The standalone tablet: the same record and lifecycle parts the engine runs, or code of its own. It is decided in the rounds on how the engine holds the game's state and on where authority lives across devices.

How a networked game carries on without the show machine, and comes back together afterwards: you choose among the panel's designs inside the rounds on how the engine holds the game's state and where authority lives. Whatever is built must not make a mixed game by accident ([[dec:standalone-games-declared-never-mixed]]).
The scoreboard: one page shown in two places, the TV's browser and the second scoreboard screen, or a view inside the GM app. It is decided in the round on how games and venues extend the engine.

The config tool, the designer's and venue technician's tool: a separate program that talks to the engine only by sending it requests, never by writing its files, or pages the engine itself serves. It is decided in the round on how one engine runs as many separate copies.

How a changed pack is taken up between games with no restart. That is not built yet; the requirements allow a change only before a game starts or after it ends. It is decided in the round on how the engine holds the game's state.

Where the setting lives that says whether the engine starts each outside program or uses one already running: in the venue technician's profile, as the earlier candidate has it, or in a file of its own, as the list of planned capabilities drawn from the roadmap has it. It is decided in the round on how games and venues extend the engine.

Where a production's own settings live (its kit's devices and phones, how long it keeps records): in the venue profile, in per-kit settings, or in both. It is decided in the round on how games and venues extend the engine. The hardware the roadmap names as required at each of its stages, and the hardware it supports, comes to you with the build plan, as the agent's call “[[call:the-design-allows-other-hardware-what-the-first-release-requires-comes-with-the-build-plan]]” says ([[dec:the-engine-is-hardware-flexible-the-roadmap-sets-the-bounds]], [[dec:the-engine-says-what-is-fixed-and-what-each-production-sets]]).

The order of the build half's work: by part (the earlier candidate put [[part:P13]] and [[part:P6]] first, since most flaws fall to them) or block by block, in the roadmap's order. The build plan, which starts with a thin first version, settles it after the design rounds.

Whether paper documents join the pack, with “unlocked” recorded during play, so the night's record can say which documents the players opened. “[[dec:the-night-s-record-and-the-after-game-article]]” left this open; today the director marks them by hand after the show. It is yours to answer, and it comes to you as a question in the round on how games and venues extend the engine.

How your answers to “How an extension for all games reaches a production” and “What a game's maker may build inside the pack” are built: the pack's format for what a maker declares, the places an add-on plugs into, and which piece each kind of extension changes in the design (the pack, the engine's code, an added outside service) ([[dec:two-kinds-of-game-extension]]), in the round on how games and venues extend the engine, with the protocol's form.

entries.title: Design for the long term, beyond ALN
entries.line: The pass designs the best architecture for the engine's next iteration, for long-term use as it grows beyond ALN; the fixes and findings from the show machine in use now are clues to where today's design is off, never the driver.

entries.title: The architecture pass is the work now
entries.line: The pass is the current work, design half first, and covers the whole engine: the engine's server, the GM scanner, the two player scanners, the scoreboards and the config tool; today's engine keeps running the game on the show machine in use now until the new engine is ready to swap in on the new show machine, and no date governs the work.

entries.title: Fixes to today's engine are evidence of design causes
entries.line: The fixes made on the show machine in use now, and the findings left unfixed there, are evidence of where today's design is weak, never the driver; fixes that share a cause become one design decision, and the sixteen design flaws are test situations every design is checked against.

entries.title: Four words for the game's live facts
entries.line: Runtime state (every fact about a running game that can change during it), authority (the place that decides a fact), copy (that fact held anywhere else) and delivery path (its route from the authority to a screen) are in the glossary; an outside program can be an authority.

entries.title: Promises, qualities, moments, venue technician
entries.line: A promise is what a person can count on at a given moment; parts keep promises and design flaws break them; a quality is something every part must have so a promise holds everywhere; a moment is when a promise matters; the person who fits a kit to a venue is the venue technician; promises carry titles only.

entries.title: Name each step by what it does
entries.line: The pass has a design half and a build half; its steps are the requirements, the panel, the design rounds, the build plan, the hostile review, the final questions and your sign-off; blocks go by name, question rounds by date and test levels by name.

entries.title: The nine questions the pass answers
entries.line: The pass answers nine questions for the whole engine, from who decides each fact to whether a reconnecting screen's catch-up is built like its live update; the nine stand, and since the design went top-down they serve as checks on each design, a reading the agent confirms as its call, listed above.

entries.title: The role question starts from settled roles
entries.line: The components keep their settled roles: the player scanners show token content and report scans, with no scoring and no live game feed; the GM scanner is the command center; the scoreboards show the public results; the question on roles starts from these.

entries.title: Standalone games: declared, never mixed
entries.line: A game can be designed and set up to run with no show machine, for a room where a network connection is not feasible or where other logistics make it better to use only GM scanners, player scanners (phone or hardware) or both; a game declares it, and no game mixes networked and standalone devices; standalone games join the list every design choice must serve. Your words of 2026-11-02 answer the hardware scanner's standalone mode: it plays standalone games as the phone's scanner does. Where the declaration is held is for the design rounds; which standalone games the engine must run is your question above. Two readings of this decision are listed above for you to confirm, and what a standalone game does with a need it cannot meet is the agent's call “[[call:a-standalone-game-follows-the-rule-you-ratified-for-missing-equipment]]”, listed above.

entries.title: The night's record and the after-game article
entries.line: What the players receive after the show is the game's business, outside the engine; the second half of the promise “[[promise:J3]]” names the director and the players after the show; the night's record carries the pack the game ran and the texts the players saw; players' emails stay outside the engine; the Director Console stays a separate program that reads the record; the two clocks (a sale stamped with the tablet's time, an adjustment with the engine computer's) join the flaw “[[flaw:C9]]”.

entries.title: One published protocol and an outside test bench
entries.line: One published, versioned protocol defines everything that crosses the engine's edge, the files that carry a game or a night included, and is designed in an early design round; the tests become a test bench outside the engine; proving each change before it reaches a show stays a quality every part must meet. Together they replace the earlier candidate's part “Joins and proofs”.

entries.title: No technical failure stops a game
entries.line: A lost connection or a device that goes down mid-game must not stop the game; at that moment the GMs must know the fallbacks that keep it running, with as little effect on the players as possible. Three readings follow, listed above for you to confirm: a device that goes down includes the show machine itself; a networked game that carries on from its devices stays the networked game it was declared as; and the engine may not make a second machine a requirement, while a game that needs the show machine by its nature may end in an orderly way. What a cut-off tablet does with a scan is your question “A GM tablet cut off from the engine” above. The quality target “[[qt:QT44]]” is the test.

entries.title: The engine is hardware-flexible; the roadmap sets the bounds
entries.line: The hardware is fixed only in that ALN runs on the kit you bought; the mature engine is flexible about hardware, so the fundamental architecture must allow that flexibility later; the current roadmap sets realistic bounds on how much of it is built now and where it names specific hardware requirements. Where the line falls is open, for the design rounds and the build plan; how it comes to you is the agent's call “[[call:the-design-allows-other-hardware-what-the-first-release-requires-comes-with-the-build-plan]]”, listed above.

entries.title: Two kinds of game extension
entries.line: A mechanic built from what the engine can already do (a new action for the players, or a new way the game responds to a trigger the engine already has) should probably be the game's own maker's work, inside the game, perhaps shared with other makers later; your example is players changing the room's lighting by scanning tokens. A response the engine cannot give yet probably needs a developer's addition for every game; your example is a service for audio in several rooms. Your wording is tentative and the record keeps it so. What a maker may build inside the pack, and how an extension for all games reaches a production, are your questions above.

entries.title: The engine says what is fixed and what each production sets
entries.line: The engine stays agnostic about any one production's numbers (the devices and phones in a kit, power-on to a running show, set-up time, how long records are kept) and says which requirements are fixed and what each production sets for itself, so an adopter can fit it to their venue; ALN is the first production: one game, one venue, the hardware you bought. The sorting of the quality targets' numbers that follows is the agent's call, listed above.

decided.topic: How the design is made, and in what order

entries.title: One program: design half, then build half
entries.line: The design half decides the shared design choices with you, one question round at a time, and ends with the new roadmap; the build half changes the engine one area at a time, starting with a thin first version on a new test bench. That an area no longer starts with its test failing on today's engine is a reading the agent confirms as its call, listed above.

entries.title: Run the pass like the re-charter
entries.line: The pass is a roadmap revision run the way the September re-charter ran: evidence, a draft with questions, a hostile review, question rounds, your sign-off; its roadmap becomes the roadmap's next revision, and on your pages the questions go by title.

entries.title: The truth sweep's charter is retired
entries.line: The truth sweep's charter is retired; its purpose, proving that every screen tells the truth, moves into the build work the pass plans, and its survey of every screen and its five recorded bugs where a screen fell out of step with the engine are evidence for the pass.

entries.title: Five documents the design half hands over
entries.line: The design half hands over the design choices with proof tests in plain words, the review that named the design flaws with every fix and finding assigned or set aside, the published protocol in place of separate proposals for the message lists, one decision note per hard-to-reverse choice, and the new roadmap; the two parts read as overtaken are confirmed as the agent's call, listed above.

entries.title: The design half's method and tools
entries.line: The design half's order is the review that named the design flaws (done), the requirements, the panel, the design rounds, the build plan, the hostile review, the final questions and your sign-off; each round writes two or three designs side by side, published as pages for you and checked against the promises, the quality targets, the extension cases and the sixteen design flaws.

entries.title: When the design half is finished
entries.line: The design half ends at your sign-off once every finding and every fix made on the show machine in use now is assigned or set aside with a reason, every design choice says how it serves the planned capabilities and standalone games, and the hostile review's blocking findings are resolved; the two earlier conditions (one design choice per question, and the rig reproducing each finding marked for live proof) are read as overtaken, which the agent confirms as its call, listed above.

entries.title: Corrections to the readers and the hardening pieces
entries.line: The pieces of the hardening block already built (the kinds of equipment a pack can ask for and a venue profile can name, the code that marks equipment not installed tonight, and the smallest test set-up) stay in the engine, and the build half changes them only where a rule requires; the review's reading of today's code was split by source, merged by cause and checked, and that work is done.

entries.title: Build the test rig when building starts
entries.line: The test rig is built at the start of building, as part of the new test bench where a thin first version of the new design runs end to end, not before design; the exception is a move that changes today's engine in place. The question on how much the rig proves before design is withdrawn.

entries.title: Design top-down, hardest-to-reverse choices first
entries.line: The rest of the design half goes top-down: finish the requirements, then design rounds ordered by the hardest decisions to reverse (the six under “Coming in the design rounds”), each with two or three designs checked against the requirements and the sixteen design flaws, then a build plan that starts with a thin first version; this site is reframed to the long-term frame.

entries.title: Independent architects propose the top-level design
entries.line: An independent panel of architects, who have not seen the reasoning of the agent running the pass, proposes and stress-tests the top-level design decisions before the first design round; its brief comes to you first.

entries.title: What the architects' panel sees, and when
entries.line: In the blind round the panel gets the goal, the requirements and the setting; only after its first proposals does it get today's engine as facts and the sixteen design flaws as test situations; withheld are the recommendations of the agent running the pass, the earlier candidate (it enters the second round as one more proposal) and the earlier lists of design choices. It runs after you review the requirements, as the agent reads your ruling “[[dec:the-decisions-page-holds-only-your-decisions]]”. Whether it also gets your binding decisions and the decisions ahead is your question above.

entries.title: The owner's site: five linked pages
entries.line: Your site was five linked pages built from one set of data (the engine, decisions, promises, parts and design flaws), with earlier wordings and changes kept in a change log; nothing in the single page it replaced had to stay. The same decision asked for the long-term frame and titles in place of numbers, and version 9, built 2026-11-01 and published 2026-11-02, did both with six pages.

entries.title: The Decisions page holds only your decisions
entries.line: This page asks you only what you alone can decide, each question explained by what it means in practice; choices that are the agent's to make (how the requirements are worded and grouped, how the panel runs, technical defaults, and readings that follow from your earlier decisions) are listed as the agent's calls with their reasons, for you to overrule; the requirements are offered for review, not as decisions.

entries.title: The new show machine's follow-ups ship when the definition session ends
entries.line: The new show machine's three follow-ups (a false boot warning on a correctly built new machine, two lines missing from the settings template, an install instruction the new operating system refuses) shipped as one small task when the definition session ended, on 2026-10-30.

entries.title: Decide in question rounds, never at sign-off
entries.line: Every decision is made in a question round with the evidence in view and written into its document at once; documents record decisions and never make them; anything new found while writing comes back to you as a question; your sign-off is a skim with no new decisions.

entries.title: The owner ratified the program document
entries.line: You ratified the program document, the plan for the architecture pass, on 2026-10-30; the definition session closed and the pass became the current work, design half first.

entries.title: No rule for documents: fix as we go
entries.line: The pass has no rule for written documents (guides, READMEs, contracts, code comments) that disagree with the code; they are fixed as we go, by the same piece of work that finds the disagreement; dated records stay as written.

entries.title: Titles, not numbers, and a topic record
entries.line: Decisions, questions and design flaws go by short plain titles in conversation and on your pages, ids stay inside records, and the decision record is reorganized by topic, each decision written as current truth with a dated history beneath.
